The Hairy-footed gerbil (Gerbillurus paeba) is a small, nocturnal rodent endemic to the coastal dune systems and sandy plains of southern Africa. In captivity, neonates emerge altricial and exceptionally lightweight, with a recorded wet weight at birth of just 2.7 grams [Wwb = 2.7 grams]. This diminutive birth mass is characteristic of the Gerbillinae subfamily and reflects the relatively short gestation period measured for this species. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable ambient temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the typical duration of pregnancy in Gerbillurus paeba lasts approximately 21 days [tg = approximately 21 days], though some field observations suggest that gestation may extend to between 46 and 49 days when females are subject to environmental stressors. This compressed pregnancy period places the species among the faster-reproducing small mammals within its arid habitat, facilitating rapid population turnover in response to ephemeral resource pulses. The low birth weight also imposes a high degree of maternal investment during the subsequent lactation phase, as the altricial newborn pup requires considerable thermal and nutritional support to achieve independent thermoregulation.

The neonatal stage is quickly followed by a period of rapid somatic growth during which the suckling juvenile relies entirely on maternal milk. At a constant environmental temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the time since birth at weaning is approximately 20 days [tx = approximately 20 days], marking the point at which the young gerbil begins to consume solid food and achieves nutritional independence. This relatively early weaning age is consistent with the life-history strategy of many desert-adapted rodents, which prioritize accelerated development to reduce the window of vulnerability during early life. Following weaning, the juvenile enters a phase of intense foraging and growth, gradually acquiring the body mass necessary for survival. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults in captivity, reflecting the asymptotic body mass, is approximately 38 grams [Wwi = approximately 38 grams]. This modest adult mass, combined with the species' small size at birth, indicates a roughly fourteen-fold increase from neonate to adult, a growth trajectory that demands efficient resource assimilation during the brief post-weaning period.

Sexual maturation in Gerbillurus paeba occurs after a well-defined developmental interval following birth. Under the stable thermal regime of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the time since birth at puberty is recorded as 63 days after birth [tp = 63 days after birth], a value that places the onset of reproductive capability relatively early in the species' life span. This pubertal timing, coinciding with the attainment of nearly full adult body mass, allows young individuals to enter the breeding population swiftly after weaning. Once sexually mature, females exhibit a remarkable reproductive output. The maximum reproductive rate for this species is achieved through a combination of modest litter size and frequent breeding events. Females typically produce 2 to 3 pups per litter [N_R_i = 2 to 3 pups per litter], with the capacity for multiple parturitions across the year. Given the brief gestation and rapid development, females can initiate a new pregnancy soon after weaning a previous litter, resulting in an estimated annual reproductive frequency of approximately 2.5 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 2.5 litters per year] under optimal conditions.

The longevity of Gerbillurus paeba in a controlled captive environment, when maintained at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], has been documented at roughly 6 years [am = roughly 6 years]. This life span is relatively extended for a small rodent, particularly one inhabiting the harsh, resource-variable dune ecosystems of the Namib and Kalahari. The combination of a six-year maximal longevity with precocious sexual maturation at 63 days after birth results in an extended window for repeated reproductive contributions. Over the course of a lifetime, a single female can produce numerous litters, each containing 2 to 3 offspring, thereby generating a substantial cumulative fecundity. The species' life-history strategy thus appears to balance a modest per-event reproductive output with a long reproductive tenure, a pattern that contrasts with the "live fast, die young" syndrome typical of many other small desert mammals. This extended life span likely evolved as a buffer against highly stochastic environmental conditions that can delay or prevent successful breeding in unfavorable years.

Comparative studies with other gerbil species reveal notable differences in physiological and life-history parameters. The neonatal mass of 2.7 grams [Wwb = 2.7 grams] is similar to that of the larger Tatera leucogaster, although the latter achieves a greater asymptotic mass. The adult body size of Gerbillurus paeba, with a maximum recorded wet weight of 38 grams [Wwi = 38 grams], positions it as a mid-sized member of its genus. Ecologically, the species is primarily granivorous, caching seeds during periods of abundance, a behavior that supports its relatively high reproductive frequency of 2.5 litters per year [F_R_i = 2.5 litters per year] and the consistent production of 2 to 3 pups per litter [N_R_i = 2 to 3 pups per litter]. Field studies conducted in the dunefields of the Namib Desert have corroborated the captive-derived weaning time of 20 days after birth [tx = 20 days after birth], although wild pups may experience slight delays depending on maternal condition and food availability at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. The gestation period under field conditions has been reported to be longer than the 21 days [tg = 21 days] observed in the lab at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], potentially due to thermal variability or nutritional stress.
